Department of Pediatrics, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center Dallas United States ([ROR:05byvp690](https://ror.org/05byvp690)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a common and progressive spinal deformity in children that exhibits striking sexual dimorphism, with girls at more than fivefold greater risk of severe disease compared to boys. Despite its medical impact, the molecular mechanisms that drive AIS are largely unknown. We previously defined a female-specific AIS genetic risk locus in an enhancer near the PAX1 gene. Here, we sought to define the roles of PAX1 and newly identified AIS-associated genes in the developmental mechanism of AIS. In a genetic study of 10,519 individuals with AIS and 93,238 unaffected controls, significant association was identified with a variant in COL11A1 encoding collagen (α1) XI (rs3753841; NM_080629.2_c.4004C>T; p.(Pro1335Leu); p=7.07E–11, OR = 1.118). Using CRISPR mutagenesis we generated Pax1 knockout mice (Pax1-/-). In postnatal spines we found that PAX1 and collagen (α1) XI protein both localize within the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region encompassing the growth plate, with less collagen (α1) XI detected in Pax1-/- spines compared to wild-type. By genetic targeting we found that wild-type Col11a1 expression in costal chondrocytes suppresses expression of Pax1 and of Mmp3, encoding the matrix metalloproteinase 3 enzyme implicated in matrix remodeling. However, the latter suppression was abrogated in the presence of the AIS-associated COL11A1P1335L mutant. Further, we found that either knockdown of the estrogen receptor gene Esr2 or tamoxifen treatment significantly altered Col11a1 and Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes. We propose a new molecular model of AIS pathogenesis wherein genetic variation and estrogen signaling increase disease susceptibility by altering a PAX1-COL11a1-MMP3 signaling axis in spinal chondrocytes. ## Introduction The human spinal column is a dynamic, segmented, bony, and cartilaginous structure that is essential for integrating the brain and nervous system with the axial skeleton while simultaneously providing flexibility in three dimensions (Richards et al., 2020). Idiopathic scoliosis is the most common developmental disorder of the spine, typically appearing during the adolescent growth spurt. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is reported in all major ancestral groups, with a population prevalence of 1.5–3% (Wise, 2014; Hresko, 2013). Children with AIS usually present with a characteristic right-thoracic major curve pattern and a compensatory lumbar curve. Major thoracolumbar and lumbar curves are less frequent (Richards et al., 2020). The three-dimensional nature of the deformity results in torsion in the spine that is most significant at the apex of the major curve, and changes in the structures of the vertebrae and ribs may develop as the curve worsens or progresses (Richards et al., 2020). Children with thoracic curves, with larger curves at first presentation, and/or with greater remaining growth potential are at increased risk of progression, but this risk decreases sharply after skeletal maturity (Richards et al., 2020). Sex is a recognized risk factor for AIS, with girls having at least a fivefold greater risk of progressive deformity requiring treatment compared to boys (Karol et al., 1993). This well-documented sexual dimorphism has prompted speculation that levels of circulating endocrine hormones, particularly estrogen, are important exposures in AIS susceptibility (Liang et al., 2021). The genetic architecture of human AIS is complex, and underlying disease mechanisms remain uncertain. Heritability studies of Northern European (Wynne-Davies, 1968; Grauers et al., 2012), North American (Riseborough and Wynne-Davies, 1973; Kruse et al., 2012), and South Asian (Tang et al., 2012) ancestral groups suggest that disease risk is multifactorial, caused by genetic and environmental contributions (Wise, 2014; Wise et al., 2020). Accordingly, population-based genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in multiple ancestral groups have identified several AIS-associated susceptibility loci, mostly within non-coding genomic regions (Wise et al., 2020). In particular, multiple GWAS have implicated non-coding regions near the LBX1 (Takahashi et al., 2011), ADGRG6 (also known as GRP126) (Kou et al., 2013), and BNC2 (Ogura et al., 2015) genes. An association with alleles in an enhancer distal to PAX1, encoding the transcription factor paired box 1, was primarily driven by females, suggesting that it contributes to the sexual dimorphism observed in AIS (Sharma et al., 2015). Subsequent meta-analysis of combined AIS GWAS identified additional susceptibility loci. These included variants in an intron of SOX6, a transcription factor, that along with PAX1, is important in early spinal column formation (Smits and Lefebvre, 2003). Furthermore, gene enrichment analyses found significant correlation of AIS-associated loci with biological pathways involving cartilage and connective tissue development (Khanshour et al., 2018). A more recent GWAS in a Japanese population identified 14 additional AIS loci that are candidates for further evaluation (Kou et al., 2019). In separate studies, genome sequencing in AIS cases and families identified enrichment of rare variants in the COL11A2 (Haller et al., 2016) and HSPG2 (Baschal et al., 2014) genes, encoding components of the cartilage extracellular matrix (ECM). Hence, variation affecting cartilage and connective tissue ECM is an emerging theme in the heterogeneous genetic architecture of AIS. Pre-clinical animal models are essential tools for accelerating mechanistic understanding of AIS and for therapeutic testing (Wise et al., 2020). In zebrafish, several genetic mutants with larval or later-onset spinal deformity have been described, including ptk7 (Hayes et al., 2014; Van Gennip et al., 2018), c21orf59 (Jaffe et al., 2016), ccdc40 (Becker-Heck et al., 2011), ccdc151 (Bachmann-Gagescu et al., 2011), dyx1c1, and kif6 (Konjikusic et al., 2018). In rescue experiments, Rebello et al. recently showed that missense variants in COL11A2 associated with human congenital scoliosis fail to rescue a vertebral malformation phenotype in a zebrafish col11a2 knockout line (Rebello et al., 2023). In mouse, conditional deletion of Adgrg6 in skeletal cartilage (using Col2a1-Cre) produces a progressive scoliosis of the thoracic spine during postnatal development that is marked by herniations within the cartilaginous endplates of involved vertebrae. Progressive scoliosis, albeit to a lesser extent, was also observed when Adgrg6 was deleted from committed chondrocytes (using ATC:Cre) (Long et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021). These studies demonstrate that cartilage and possibly other osteochondroprogenitor cells contribute to the scoliosis phenotype in these models (Liu et al., 2019). Taken together, genetic and functional studies in mouse, although limited, support the hypothesis that deficiencies in biogenesis and/or homeostasis of cartilage, intervertebral disc (IVD), and dense connective tissues undermine the maintenance of proper spinal alignment during the adolescent growth spurt (Wise et al., 2020). The combined contribution of reported AIS-associated variants is broadly estimated to account for less than 10% of the overall genetic risk of the disease (Kou et al., 2019). To address this knowledge gap, we sought to define novel loci associated with AIS susceptibility in genes encoding proteins of the ECM (i.e. the ‘matrisome’; Naba et al., 2012b; Naba et al., 2012a). Here, we identify new genetic associations with AIS. Further, our functional assessments support a new disease model wherein AIS-associated genetic variation and estrogen signaling perturb a PAX1-COL11a1-MMP3 axis in chondrocytes. ## Results ### Nonsynonymous variants in matrisome genes are associated with increased risk of AIS The ‘matrisome’ has been defined as ‘all genes encoding structural ECM components and those encoding proteins that may interact with or remodel the ECM’ (Hynes and Naba, 2012). Proteins comprising the global ECM as currently defined have been identified by both experimental and bioinformatic methods (Naba et al., 2012b). We assembled 1027 matrisome genes as previously identified (Naba et al., 2016), including 274 core-matrisome and 753 matrisome-associated genes (N=1027 total). For the genes encoding these 1027 proteins, we identified all nonsynonymous common variants (MAF>0.01) queried by the Illumina HumanCoreExome-24v1.0 beadchip and determined their genotypes in a discovery cohort of 1358 cases and 12,507 controls, each of European ancestry (Table 1). After applying multiple quality control measures (see Methods section), we retained 2008 variants in 597 matrisome genes for association testing (Supplementary file 1). This sample size was estimated to provide at least 80% power to detect significant associations at the matrisome-wide level (α≤2.5E–05), for alleles with population frequency ≥0.05 and OR ≥1.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). Two nonsynonymous variants, in COL11A1 (rs3753841; NM_080629.2_c.4004C>T; p.(Pro1335Leu); odds ratio (OR)=1.236 [95% CI = 1.134–1.347], p=1.17E–06) and MMP14 (rs1042704; NM_004995.4_c.817G>A; p.(Asp273Asn); OR = 1.239 [95% CI = 1.125–1.363], p=1.89E–05) were significantly associated with AIS (Figure 1A). Given the sexual dimorphism in AIS and our prior observation of a female-predominant disease locus (Sharma et al., 2015), we tested the 2008 variants separately in females (N=1157 cases and 7138 controls). In females, the association with rs3753841 remained statistically significant, whereas rs1042704, near MMP14, was not associated with AIS in females (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). Our study was not sufficiently powered to test males separately. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89762/elife-89762-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) Manhattan plot showing –log10 p-values (y-axis) versus chromosomal position (x-axis) for the 2008 common coding variants tested in the discovery study USA (TX). _USA (TX): Texas cohort; USA (MO): Missouri cohort; SW-D: Danish cohort; JP: Japanese cohort; HK: Hong Kong cohort; NHW: Non-Hispanic White; EAS: East Asian._ To validate these results, we sought to replicate the associations of rs3753841 and rs1042704 in four independent AIS case-control cohorts, from North America, Europe, and eastern Asia, representing multiple ethnicities (total N=9161 AIS cases, 80,731 healthy controls, Table 1). Genotypes for both variants were extracted from these datasets and tested for association by meta-analysis together with the discovery cohort (see Methods). Meta-analysis of all cohorts together increased the evidence for association of both variants with AIS risk (Figure 1B). While a similar effect size was noted for rs1042704 in Japanese and Han Chinese cohorts, the results were less significant, likely due to lower minor allele frequencies (East Asian MAF = 0.02 compared to total non-Asian cohort MAF = 0.20) in these populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3). Plotting recombination across both regions suggested that these signals were likely confined to blocks of linkage disequilibrium within the COL11A1 and MMP14 genes, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). Rare dominant mutations in COL11A1, often disrupting a Gly-X-Y sequence, can cause Marshall (MRSHS) (OMIM #154780) or Stickler syndromes (STL2) (OMIM #604841) marked variously by facial anomalies, sensineural hearing loss, short stature, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, eye anomalies, ectodermal features, and scoliosis. Notably, our AIS cohort and particularly individuals carrying the rs3753841 risk allele were negative for co-morbidities or obvious features of Marshall or Stickler syndromes. Thus, variation in COL11A1 is independently associated with AIS. Notably, we did not detect common variants in linkage disequilibrium (R2>0.6) with the top SNP rs3753841 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). Further, analysis of 625 exomes from the discovery cohort (46%) identified only three rare COL11A1 variants in five individuals (Supplementary file 2), and rare variant burden testing for COL11A1 was not significant as expected (data not shown). These observations suggested that rs3753841 itself could confer disease risk, although our methods would not detect deep intronic variants that could contribute to the overall association signal. ### COL11A1 is expressed in adolescent spinal tissues We next characterized COL11A1 in postnatal spine development. COL11A1 encodes one of three alpha chains of type XI collagen, a member of the fibrillar collagen subgroup and regulator of nucleation and initial fibril assembly, particularly in cartilage (Fernandes et al., 2007). Spinal deformity is well described in Col11a1-deficient (cho/cho) embryos (Hafez et al., 2015; Seegmiller et al., 1971). In mouse tendon, Col11a1 mRNA is abundant during development but barely detectable at 3 months of age (Wenstrup et al., 2011). We analyzed RNAseq datasets derived from adolescent human spinal tissues (Makki et al., 2020), finding that COL11A1 was upregulated in cartilage relative to bone and muscle. In cartilage, PAX1 and COL11A2 showed the strongest expression levels relative to other published human AIS-associated genes (Kou et al., 2013; Ogura et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2015; Khanshour et al., 2018; Haller et al., 2016; Baschal et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2007; Figure 2A). In all, most AIS-associated genes showed the strongest expression levels in cartilage relative to other adolescent spinal tissues. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89762/elife-89762-fig2-v1.jpg) **Figure 2.:** (A) A heatmap of transcript per million (TPM) values of COL11A1, MMP14, and other published genes associated with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). The average TPM value of matrisome genes is represented as MATRISOME. (B) Detection of collagen a1(XI) in P0.5 mouse spine. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) shown at top, with immunofluorescence (IF) staining below. ‘-ab’ refers to negative controls lacking primary antibody (shown at left). Results are representative of N≥3 technical replicates in whole spines. (C) Detection of collagen a1(XI) in P28 mouse spine. Negative antibody IHC control shown at left; antibody-positive IHC shown at right. Enlarged, rotated view of white boxed area shows a biphasic staining pattern. CEP – cartilage endplate; GP – growth plate. Results are representative of N≥3 technical replicates in whole spines. ![Figure 2—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89762/elife-89762-fig2-figsupp1-v1.jpg) **Figure 2—figure supplement 1.:** Boxed area shows biphasic staining pattern expanded at right. R – presumed resting zone; P – columnar chondrocytes of presumed proliferating zone; H – presumed hypertrophic zone and chondro-osseous junction. Each image is representative of results in at least three animals. We next sought to characterize Col11a1 expression in spines of postnatal mice. To detect COL11A1 protein (collagen α1(XI)), we performed immunohistochemistry (IHC) and immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy using a collagen α1(XI) reactive antibody (Sun et al., 2020) in newborn (P0.5) and adolescent (P28) mice. In spines of P0.5 mice, strong staining was observed in the nucleus pulposus (NP) and in surrounding annulus fibrosus (AF) (Figure 2B). In thoracic spines of P28 mice, the compartments of the IVD were more distinct, and strong collagen α1(XI) staining was observed in each (Figure 2C). In regions of the cartilage endplate (CEP)-vertebral bone transition, collagen α1(XI) was detected in columnar chondrocytes, particularly in the hypertrophic zone adjacent to condensing bone (Figure 2C). We also examined collagen α1(XI) expression in ribs, as these structures are also involved in the scoliotic deformity (Richards et al., 2020). In P28 rib growth plates, as in spine, a biphasic pattern was observed in which collagen α1(XI) reactivity was most pronounced around cells of the presumed resting and pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic zones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). These data show that in mouse, collagen α1(XI) is detectable in all compartments of young postnatal IVD and, at the thoracic level, is particularly abundant in the chondro-osseous junction region of IVD and vertebral growth plate. ### Col11a1 is downregulated in the absence of Pax1 in mouse spine and tail We previously identified AIS-associated variants within a putative enhancer of PAX1 encoding the transcription factor Paired Box 1 (Sharma et al., 2015; Khanshour et al., 2018). Pax1 is a well-described marker of condensing sclerotomal cells as they form segments that will eventually become the IVD and vertebrae of the spine (Chan et al., 2014; Aszódi et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2011). We generated Pax1 knockout mice (Pax1-/-) using CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis and validated them using sequencing and southern blot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Homozygous Pax1-/- mice were viable and developed spine deformity and kinks in the tail, as observed in other Pax1-deficient mice (Wilm et al., 1998). We next compared the expression of collagen α1(XI) protein in IVD and condensing bone of wild-type and Pax1-/- mice by performing IF staining in P28 spines (Figure 3A). In wild-type IVD, strong overlapping expression of collagen α1(XI) and PAX1 cells was observed, mostly within the CEP and chondro-osseous interface (Figure 3A). PAX1 staining was negative in Pax1-/- mice as expected, and collagen α1(XI) staining was dramatically diminished in CEP and the chondro-osseous vertebral borders. Moreover, the IVD in Pax1-/- mice was highly disorganized, without discernable NP, AF, and CEP structures as has been reported (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Wallin et al., 1994). To test the effect of Pax1 on expression of Col11a1 and other AIS-associated genes during embryonic development, RNA was isolated from vertebral tissue dissected from the tails of embryonic stage 12.5 (E12.5) wild-type and Pax1-/- mice and subjected to bulk RNAseq and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) (Figure 3B). Gene-set enrichment analysis of RNAseq was most significant for the gene ontology term ‘extracellular matrix’ (Figure 3C). By qRT-PCR analysis, expression of Col11a1, Adgrg6, and Sox6 was significantly reduced in female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice (Figure 3D–G). These data show that loss of Pax1 leads to reduced expression of Col11a1 and the AIS-associated genes Adgrg6 and Sox6 in affected tissue of the developing tail. ![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89762/elife-89762-fig3-v1.jpg) **Figure 3.:** (A) Immunofluorescence (IF) staining of P28 intervertebral disc (IVD) from thoracic regions of Pax1-/- (bottom) and wild-type (WT) littermate (middle, top) mice using PAX1- (green) and collagen a1(XI)-specific (red) antibodies and DAPI nuclear counterstain. (D) Pax1-/- mice showed kinky tail phenotype on dorsal (left) and lateral (right) views. ![Figure 3—figure supplement 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89762/elife-89762-fig3-figsupp2-v1.jpg) ### Col11a1 regulates Mmp3 expression in chondrocytes COL11A1 has been linked with ECM remodeling and invasiveness in some cancers (Wu et al., 2014). In solid tumors, COL11A1 has been shown to alter ECM remodeling by enhancing MMP3 expression in response to TGFΒ1 (Wu et al., 2014). MMP3 encodes matrix metalloproteinase 3, also known as stromolysin, an enzyme implicated in matrix degradation and remodeling in connective tissues (Mudgett et al., 1998). We confirmed strong MMP3 mRNA expression, relative to COL11A1, in human spinal cartilage and bone, but minimal expression in spinal muscle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). We next cultured costal chondrocytes from P0.5 Col11a1fl/fl mice (Sun et al., 2020) and subsequently removed Col11a1 by treating with Cre-expressing adenoviruses. After confirming Col11a1 excision (Figure 4A), we compared Mmp3 expression in these cells to cells treated with GFP-expressing adenoviruses lacking Cre activity. We found that Mmp3 expression was significantly increased in cells where Col11a1 mRNA expression was downregulated by about 70% compared to untreated cells (Figure 4B). Furthermore, western blotting in these cells demonstrated an ~2- to 5-fold increase in pro-, secreted, and active forms of Mmp3 protein when collagen α1(XI) was reduced. The proteolytic processing per se of precursor MMP3 into active forms (Sun et al., 2014) did not appear to be affected by Col11a1 expression (Figure 4C). These results suggest that Mmp3 expression is negatively regulated by Col11a1 in mouse costal chondrocytes. ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89762/elife-89762-fig4-v1.jpg) **Figure 4.:** (A) PCR assay of Col11a1 excision in Col11a1fl/fl cultured costal chondrocytes. To test whether Col11a1 affects Mmp3 expression in vivo, we bred Col11a1fl/fl female mice with Col11a1fl/fl:ATC males carrying the Acan enhancer-driven, doxycycline-inducible Cre (ATC) transgene (Dy et al., 2012). ATC has been shown to harbor Cre-mediated recombination activity in most differentiated chondrocytes and in NP within 2 days of treating pregnant mothers with doxycycline starting at E15.5 (Dy et al., 2012). ATC activity was confirmed by crossing this line to the R26td[Tomato] reporter that ubiquitously expresses the fluorescent gene Tomato after Cre recombination. Strong Cre activity was seen in P0 pups of mothers treated with doxycycline at E15.5 in the NP, CEP, and AF of the IVD and in chondrocytes of the growth plates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Pregnant Col11a1fl/fl females were treated with doxycycline water from E15.5 to induce Cre expression in differentiated chondrocytes. Given that AIS originates in children who appear to be otherwise healthy, even its tissue of origin has been difficult to discern, and long debated (Wise et al., 2020). The advent of powerful genotyping and sequencing methods in the last two decades has led to breakthrough discoveries of genetic loci associated with AIS, most in non-coding regions of the genome that are difficult to interpret biologically (Wise et al., 2020). Aggregating these results, however, provided supportive evidence that pathways of cartilage and connective tissue ECM development are relevant in AIS etiology (Wise et al., 2020; Khanshour et al., 2018). Here, in the largest multi-ethnic human cohort studied to date, we elected to test the hypothesis that alterations in ECM proteins themselves contribute to AIS susceptibility. This approach yielded most significant evidence for a common protein-altering variant in the COL11A1 gene encoding collagen α1(XI), a minor yet critical component of cartilaginous ECM. Moreover, our studies define a COL11A1-mediated disease pathway (Figure 7) and point to the chondro-osseous junction of IVD and vertebrae spine as a relevant cellular compartment in AIS etiology. ![Figure 7.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89762/elife-89762-fig7-v1.jpg) **Figure 7.:** Collagen XI is held in the pericellular space by integrins and DDR2. COL11A1, under the regulation of ESR2 and PAX1, signals through unknown mechanisms and inhibits MMP3 transcription. The results of this study together with the previous observation of COL11A2 rare variant enrichment in AIS support a role for the collagen α1(XI) heterotrimer itself in its pathogenesis (Haller et al., 2016). Collagen type XI, composed of three chains encoded by the COL11A1, COL11A2, and COL2A1 genes (OMIM #s 120280,120290, 120140, respectively), is a minor component of collagen type II fibrils that are abundant in cartilage. Collagen type XI is also broadly expressed in testis, trachea, tendons, trabecular bone, skeletal muscle, placenta, lung, brain neuroepithelium, the vitreous of the eye, and IVDs (Yoshioka et al., 1995). In the pericellular space, collagen α1(XI) initiates fibrillogenesis with collagen type II fibrils, maintaining regular spacing and diameter of the collagen fibrils, while organizing the pericellular surface by interaction with cartilage proteoglycans (Smith et al., 1989; Luo and Karsdal, 2019). Purified human collagen type XI, when added back to chondrocytes in in vitro culture, stimulates chondrogenesis while inhibiting hypertrophy, as measured by histological staining, proliferation assays, and relative expression of chondrogenic early marker genes (Li et al., 2018). In newborn and 1-month-old mice, we found that collagen α1(XI) was abundant in IVD and at the chondro-osseous junction of IVD and vertebrae, particularly concentrated in pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic chondrocytic cells. In long bone growth plates, Long et al., 2022, recently identified eight distinct cell clusters after unsupervised analysis of single cell (scRNAseq) of flow-sorted hypertrophic chondrocytes from Col10a1Cre;Rosa26fs-tdTomato mice. At E16.5, Col11a1 expression was highest in cells with signatures of pre-hypertrophic to hypertrophic transition, and lowest in cells with osteogenic signatures (M Hilton, personal communication) (Long et al., 2022). Taken together, these results suggest that collagen α1(XI) normally participates in maintaining growth plate cells in a hypertrophic, pre-osteogenic state, although little is known about its precise molecular function in that compartment, or in the IVD, during spinal development. Spines of Col11a1-deficient mice (cho/cho) show incompletely formed vertebral bodies, spinal curvatures, and decreased separation between vertebrae, which are themselves less mineralized than in wild-type mice (Hafez et al., 2015). Notably, common COL11A1 variants also have been associated with adult lumbar disc herniation and lumbar disc degeneration, as well as DXA-measured bone size, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis (Jiang et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2007; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019). Although gain-of-function or dominant-negative effects of the rs3753841 variant would not have been revealed in our assays, the spinal deformity noted in the cho/cho loss-of-function model, and failure of missense variants in Col11a2 to rescue congenital scoliosis (Rebello et al., 2023), leads us to surmise that reduction in the components of collagen type XI disrupts spinal development. Pax1 is a well-described marker of early spine development, where it activates a gene expression cascade starting at E12.5–13.5 in mouse development (Wilm et al., 1998; Rodrigo et al., 2003; Sivakamasundari et al., 2017). Our data showed that loss of Pax1 leads to decreased expression of Col11a1, Sox6, and Adgrg6 in E12.5 tails of both male and female mice. The downregulation of Col11a1 is consistent with a prior study of gene expression in flow-sorted GFP-labeled Pax1-/- embryonic IVD cells (Sivakamasundari et al., 2017). However, from these experiments we cannot discern if Pax1 directly regulates Col11a1 in cis, or by an indirect effect. It is likely, however, that Col11a1 expression in developing tail is directly activated by binding SOX transcription factors, as a prior genomic study using chromatin immunoprecipitation and sequencing in rat chondrosarcoma cells identified super enhancers near the Col11a1 gene that were bound multiple times by SOX9 and SOX6 (Liu and Lefebvre, 2015). The SOX5/6/9 trio is known to regulate many of the same genes as PAX1 (Sivakamasundari et al., 2017), but whether this includes Col11a1 is unknown. In mouse postnatal spines, we observed co-localization of collagen α1(XI) and PAX1 proteins specifically within the cartilaginous endplate-vertebral junction region that includes the vertebral growth plate. The endplate, which is important as the site allowing diffusion of nutrients from the circulation into the avascular inner IVD, harbors subpopulations of cells expressing type II collagen presumably organized by collagen type XI (Chan et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2011). While the endplate is continuous with the vertebral growth plate in mice, it is important to note that in humans the endplate and vertebrae become distinctly separate structures with closure of the growth plates at puberty (Chan et al., 2014). This is also the site of the ring apophyses that form the insertion of the IVD into vertebrae (Costa et al., 2021). Lagging maturity of the ring apophysis, combined with mechanical forces across the IVD in the horizontal plane, has been proposed as an initiating factor leading to rotatory decompensation in the adolescent spine in AIS (Costa et al., 2021; Castelein et al., 2020). Recently, Sun et al. reported the discovery of a vertebral skeletal stem cell (vSSC) residing in the endplate and marked by expression of the genes Zic1 and Pax1, along with other cell surface markers (Sun et al., 2023). These vSSCs also express high levels of Col11a1 (M Greenblatt, personal communication). It is interesting to consider that AIS-associated variation in collagenα1(XI), perhaps together with mechanical forces, could alter the differentiation trajectory of this cell niche. Altogether, extant data and our results strongly suggest that cell populations at the IVD-vertebral junction region are relevant in AIS pathogenesis. Further investigation is warranted to understand the developmental programs of cells in this region of the spine. Matrix metalloproteinase 3, also known as stromolysin, is a secreted enzyme expressed in connective tissues and in regions of endochondral ossification (Ortega et al., 2004). MMP3 has degradative activity toward a variety of ECM components, including proteoglycans, fibronectin, laminin, but notably not type I collagen (Sellers and Murphy, 1981). Additionally, in chondrocytes MMP3 also has been shown to translocate to the nucleus, where it activates transcription of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF/CCN2) by binding to an element known as transcription enhancer dominant in chondrocytes (TRENDIC) (Eguchi et al., 2008; Cui et al., 2017). Our observations of a Col11a1-Mmp3 signaling axis in chondrocytes and CEP cells raise the possibility that Col11a1 variation may have consequences for both MMP3 enzymatic activity levels and MMP3-mediated transcriptional programming in these cells. COL11A1 missense variants, usually altering glycine or proline in Gly-X-Y repeats in the collagen α1(XI) helical domain as with COL11A1P1335L, are reported to be frequent in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and have been linked to transcriptional changes and tumor invasiveness (Lee et al., 2021). The mechanisms by which chondrocytes or other cells sense such single amino acid changes in collagen α1(XI) and induce subsequent transcriptional responses are unknown but may involve direct interaction with integrins in the pericellular space (Lee et al., 2021). We found that Col11a1 expression is sensitive to estrogen receptor blockade or knockdown in chondrocytes. Type XI collagen is also a key player in organizing the pericellular space, which is critical for transmitting mechanical forces from the ECM to the cell (Xu et al., 2016). Thus, it is interesting to consider that type XI collagen may effectively act as a receptor for environmental cues, i.e., mechanical forces and estrogen signaling, in the adolescent spine. Our study provides new insights into the regulation and signaling role of Col11a1 in chondrocytes, and it suggests potential mechanisms by which its genetic variation contributes to AIS susceptibility. ## Methods ### Discovery study The cases in the discovery stage (USA TX: n=1358) were recruited at Scottish Rite for Children. Informed consent to participate in this research was obtained as approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University Texas Southwestern Medical Center, protocol STU 112010-150. Subjects were genotyped on the Illumina HumanCoreExome BeadChip (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). For controls, we utilized 12,507 non-AMD GRU (non-age-related macular degeneration general research use) subjects of the European ancestry downloaded from dbGaP website (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gap/) from the International Age-Related Macular Degeneration Genomics Consortium study (IAMDGC: phs001039.v1.p1.c1). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89762.4.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89762.4.sa1)

Summary:

This revised study follows up on previous work showing a female-specific enhancer region of PAX1 is associated with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). This new analysis combines human GWAS analysis from multiple countries to identify a new AIS-associated coding variant in the COL11A1 gene (COL11A1P1335L). Using a Pax1 knockout mouse they go on to find that PAX1 and Collagen XI protein are expressed in the intervertebral discs (IVDs) and robustly in the growth plate, showing that COL11A1 expression is reduced in Pax1 mutant growth plate. Moreover, other AIS-associated genes, Gpr126 and Sox6, were also reduced in Pax1 mutant mice, suggesting a common pathway is involved in AIS.

Using SV40 immortalized costal cartilage cells, derived from floxed Col11a1 mice primary rib cage cartilage, they go to show that removal of Col11a1 leads to reduction of Mmp3 expression. In this context, the expression of wild-type Col11a1 restored regular levels of Mmp3 expression, while expression of the AIS-associated Col11a1P1335L allele failed to restore normal Mmp3 expression. This supports a model that the AIS-associated Col11a1P1335L allele leads to the dysregulation of ECM in vivo.

Using this culture system, they go on to test the role of the estrogen receptor ESR2, showing that loss of this receptor leads to reduced Mmp3 and Pax1 expression, and increased Col11a1 expression. They support this by showing similar gene expression changes and estrogen receptor function in Rat cartilage endplate cell culture.

Altogether, this study nicely brings together an impressive number of human genetic data from multi-ethnic AIS cohorts and controls from across the globe and functionally tests these findings in cell culture and animal models. This study wonderfully integrates other findings from other human and mouse work in AIS and supports a new molecular mechanism by which estrogen can interact and synergize with COL11A1/PAX1/MMP3 signaling to change ECM development and dynamics, thus providing a tangible model for mutations and dysregulation of this pathway can increase the susceptibility of scoliosis.

Strengths:

This work integrates a large cohort of human genetic data from AIS patient and control from diverse ethnic backgrounds, across the globe. This work attempts to functionally test their findings in vivio and by use of cell culture.

Weaknesses:

Many of the main functional work was done in cell culture and not in vivo.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89762.4.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89762.4.sa2)

Summary:

In this manuscript, Yu and colleagues sought to identify new susceptibility genes for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). The significance of this work is high, especially given the still large knowledge gap of the mechanistic underpinnings for AIS. In this multidisciplinary body of work, the authors first performed a genetic association study of AIS case-control cohorts (combined 9,161 cases and 80,731 controls) which leveraged common SNPs in 1027 previously defined matrisome genes. Two nonsynonymous variants were found to be significantly associated with AIS: MMP14 p.Asp273Asn and COL11A1 p.Pro1153Leu, the latter of which had the more robust association and remained significant when females were tested independent of males. Next, the authors followed a series of functional validation experiments to support biological involvement of COL11A1 p.Pro1153Leu in AIS through expression, biochemical, and histological studies in physiologically relevant cell and mouse models. Together, the authors propose a hitherto unreported model for AIS that involves the interplay of the COL11A1 susceptibility locus with estrogen signaling to alter a Pax1-Col11a1-Mmp3 signaling axis at the growth plate.

Strengths:

The manuscript is clearly written and follows a series of logical steps toward connecting multiple matrisome genes and putative AIS effectors in a new framework of pathomechanism. The multidisciplinary nature of the work makes it a strong body of work wherein multiple models offer multiple lines of supportive data. Thus, this manuscript remains an important multidisciplinary study of the genetic and functional basis of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS). To the benefit of the overall manuscript quality, the reviewers have addressed most concerns to satisfaction. Please include the list of three rare missense variants mentioned in the response to reviewers as a supplementary table. Please also include methods for the SKATO rare variant burden analysis.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2014 and Smith et al., 2011.

claims.claim: In humans the endplate and vertebrae become distinctly separate structures with closure of the growth plates at puberty.
claims.source: While the endplate is continuous with the vertebral growth plate in mice, it is important to note that in humans the endplate and vertebrae become distinctly separate structures with closure of the growth plates at puberty (Chan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Lagging maturity of the ring apophysis, combined with mechanical forces across the IVD in the horizontal plane, has been proposed as an initiating factor leading to rotatory decompensation in the adolescent spine in AIS.
claims.source: Lagging maturity of the ring apophysis, combined with mechanical forces across the IVD in the horizontal plane, has been proposed as an initiating factor leading to rotatory decompensation in the adolescent spine in AIS (Costa et al., 2021; Castelein et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Costa et al., 2021 and Castelein et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Sun et al. reported the discovery of a vertebral skeletal stem cell (vSSC) residing in the endplate and marked by expression of the genes Zic1 and Pax1.
claims.source: Recently, Sun et al. reported the discovery of a vertebral skeletal stem cell (vSSC) residing in the endplate and marked by expression of the genes Zic1 and Pax1, along with other cell surface markers (Sun et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Vertebral skeletal stem cells (vSSCs) express high levels of Col11a1.
claims.source: These vSSCs also express high levels of Col11a1 (M Greenblatt, personal communication).
claims.evidence: This is supported by personal communication.

claims.claim: AIS-associated variation in collagen α1(XI), perhaps together with mechanical forces, could alter the differentiation trajectory of the vertebral skeletal stem cell niche.
claims.source: It is interesting to consider that AIS-associated variation in collagenα1(XI), perhaps together with mechanical forces, could alter the differentiation trajectory of this cell niche.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about vSSCs and Col11a1 expression.

claims.claim: Cell populations at the IVD-vertebral junction region are relevant in AIS pathogenesis.
claims.source: Altogether, extant data and our results strongly suggest that cell populations at the IVD-vertebral junction region are relevant in AIS pathogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization and expression data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Matrix metalloproteinase 3 is a secreted enzyme expressed in connective tissues and in regions of endochondral ossification.
claims.source: Matrix metalloproteinase 3, also known as stromolysin, is a secreted enzyme expressed in connective tissues and in regions of endochondral ossification (Ortega et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ortega et al., 2004.

claims.claim: MMP3 has degradative activity toward a variety of ECM components, including proteoglycans, fibronectin, laminin, but notably not type I collagen.
claims.source: MMP3 has degradative activity toward a variety of ECM components, including proteoglycans, fibronectin, laminin, but notably not type I collagen (Sellers and Murphy, 1981).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Sellers and Murphy, 1981.

claims.claim: In chondrocytes MMP3 has been shown to translocate to the nucleus, where it activates transcription of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF/CCN2) by binding to an element known as transcription enhancer dominant in chondrocytes (TRENDIC).
claims.source: Additionally, in chondrocytes MMP3 also has been shown to translocate to the nucleus, where it activates transcription of connective tissue growth factor (CTGF/CCN2) by binding to an element known as transcription enhancer dominant in chondrocytes (TRENDIC) (Eguchi et al., 2008; Cui et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Eguchi et al., 2008 and Cui et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Col11a1 variation may have consequences for both MMP3 enzymatic activity levels and MMP3-mediated transcriptional programming in chondrocytes and CEP cells.
claims.source: Our observations of a Col11a1-Mmp3 signaling axis in chondrocytes and CEP cells raise the possibility that Col11a1 variation may have consequences for both MMP3 enzymatic activity levels and MMP3-mediated transcriptional programming in these cells.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about Col11a1-Mmp3 regulation.

claims.claim: COL11A1 missense variants, usually altering glycine or proline in Gly-X-Y repeats in the collagen α1(XI) helical domain, are reported to be frequent in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas.
claims.source: COL11A1 missense variants, usually altering glycine or proline in Gly-X-Y repeats in the collagen α1(XI) helical domain as with COL11A1P1335L, are reported to be frequent in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and have been linked to transcriptional changes and tumor invasiveness (Lee et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claims.claim: COL11A1 missense variants have been linked to transcriptional changes and tumor invasiveness.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claims.source: The mechanisms by which chondrocytes or other cells sense such single amino acid changes in collagen α1(XI) and induce subsequent transcriptional responses are unknown but may involve direct interaction with integrins in the pericellular space (Lee et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Type XI collagen is a key player in organizing the pericellular space, which is critical for transmitting mechanical forces from the ECM to the cell.
claims.source: We found that Col11a1 expression is sensitive to estrogen receptor blockade or knockdown in chondrocytes. Type XI collagen is also a key player in organizing the pericellular space, which is critical for transmitting mechanical forces from the ECM to the cell (Xu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Type XI collagen may effectively act as a receptor for environmental cues, i.e., mechanical forces and estrogen signaling, in the adolescent spine.
claims.source: Thus, it is interesting to consider that type XI collagen may effectively act as a receptor for environmental cues, i.e., mechanical forces and estrogen signaling, in the adolescent spine.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings about Col11a1 expression and regulation.

results.result: A common nonsynonymous variant in COL11A1 (rs3753841; p.Pro1335Leu) is significantly associated with AIS risk across multiple ancestral populations, with meta-analysis yielding p=7.07E-11 and OR=1.118. The association remained significant in females but not for the MMP14 variant, and AIS patients carrying this variant lacked features of Marshall or Stickler syndromes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C52, C53, C54, C55 provide converging genetic association evidence from discovery and replication cohorts across multiple ancestries with appropriate statistical significance. Claims C58 and C59 establish that this variant is independently associated with AIS rather than syndromic scoliosis. The statistical evidence is robust with large sample sizes (N=103,757 total) and consistent effect sizes across populations.

results.result: COL11A1 is highly expressed in adolescent human spinal cartilage, and collagen α1(XI) protein localizes to all compartments of the postnatal mouse IVD, with particularly abundant expression in the chondro-osseous junction region including the cartilage endplate and growth plate, especially in pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C68 are supported by RNAseq data (C60-C62) and immunohistochemistry/immunofluorescence data (C63-C68) shown in Figure 2. The expression pattern is consistently demonstrated across multiple developmental timepoints (P0.5, P28) and anatomical locations, providing strong evidence for the tissue-specific localization of COL11A1.

results.result: Pax1 knockout mice develop spine deformity and show dramatically diminished collagen α1(XI) staining in the cartilage endplate and chondro-osseous borders. Loss of Pax1 leads to reduced expression of Col11a1, Adgrg6, and Sox6 in E12.5 tail tissue, with gene-set enrichment analysis highlighting extracellular matrix as the most significant pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C79 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including CRISPR-generated knockout mice (C70), immunofluorescence data (C71-C73), histology (C74), RNAseq and gene ontology analysis (C75), and qRT-PCR data (C76-C79) shown in Figure 3. The convergent evidence from protein localization, gene expression, and pathway analysis strongly supports the regulatory relationship between Pax1 and Col11a1.

results.result: Col11a1 negatively regulates Mmp3 expression in mouse costal chondrocytes. Knockdown of Col11a1 by ~70% resulted in significant upregulation of Mmp3 mRNA and ~2- to 5-fold increase in pro-, secreted, and active forms of Mmp3 protein, both in vitro and in vivo using conditional knockout mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 and C90 are supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data (Figure 4B-C) from in vitro Cre-mediated excision experiments, and by in vivo data from Col11a1fl/fl:ATC mice (Figure 4D). The consistent upregulation of Mmp3 upon Col11a1 reduction across both experimental systems provides strong evidence for this regulatory relationship.

results.result: The AIS-associated COL11A1P1335L variant abrogates the suppression of Mmp3 expression. While wild-type COL11A1 overexpression suppressed Mmp3, the P1335L mutant failed to downregulate Mmp3 despite being overexpressed at similar levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 and C10 are supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data from SV40-immortalized chondrocytes overexpressing wild-type or mutant COL11A1 (Figure 5A-B). The differential effect of wild-type versus mutant protein on Mmp3 expression provides functional evidence linking the AIS-associated variant to altered gene regulation. However, the mechanism by which this missense variant affects transcriptional regulation remains unclear.

results.result: Estrogen receptor signaling modulates the Col11a1-Mmp3 regulatory axis in mouse chondrocytes. Knockdown of Esr2 or tamoxifen treatment significantly upregulated Col11a1 and downregulated Mmp3 expression. Simultaneous knockdown of Col11a1 and Esr2 normalized Mmp3 levels, and Col11a1 knockdown upregulated Pax1, suggesting a negative feedback loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 and C99-C107, C111 are supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data from siRNA knockdown and tamoxifen treatment experiments (Figure 6A-B and supplement). The convergent evidence from Esr2 knockdown, pharmacological modulation, and double knockdown experiments supports the conclusion that ESR2 signaling disrupts Col11a1-mediated suppression of Mmp3 in mouse chondrocytes. However, C108-C110 show this relationship does not hold in rat CEP cells, suggesting species or cell-type specificity.

results.result: The authors propose a molecular model wherein genetic variation in COL11A1 and estrogen signaling increase AIS susceptibility by altering a PAX1-COL11A1-MMP3 signaling axis in spinal chondrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claim C15 represents an integrative model supported by the convergent evidence from genetic association (C4, C52-C55), expression and localization studies (C60-C68), Pax1 knockout experiments (C70-C79), Col11a1-Mmp3 regulatory studies (C84-C90), variant functional analysis (C95-C97), and estrogen signaling experiments (C99-C107). While each component is experimentally supported, the complete pathway and its causal role in AIS pathogenesis requires further validation, particularly in human tissues and in vivo models that recapitulate the disease phenotype.

results.result: AIS is a common spinal deformity with 1.5-3% population prevalence, characterized by right-thoracic curves and striking sexual dimorphism with girls having >5-fold greater risk of severe disease. Risk factors include thoracic curves, larger curves at presentation, and greater remaining growth potential, with risk decreasing after skeletal maturity. Estrogen is speculated to be important in AIS susceptibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C16-C26 describe established clinical and epidemiological features of AIS supported by citations to the literature (Karol et al., 1993; Richards et al., 2020; Wise, 2014; Hresko, 2013; Liang et al., 2021). These are well-documented characteristics of the disease that provide context for the study.

results.result: The genetic architecture of AIS is complex and multifactorial. Prior GWAS have identified multiple susceptibility loci in non-coding regions near LBX1, ADGRG6, BNC2, PAX1, and SOX6, with enrichment in pathways involving cartilage and connective tissue development. Rare variants in COL11A2 and HSPG2 have also been identified. Combined, reported variants account for <10% of overall genetic risk.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C44 and C50-C51 summarize prior genetic findings in AIS supported by multiple citations. These claims accurately represent the state of knowledge in the field and provide rationale for the current study's focus on matrisome genes. The characterization of AIS as having complex, heterogeneous genetic architecture with incomplete heritability explained is well-established.

results.result: Animal models support a role for cartilage and connective tissue in scoliosis pathogenesis. Zebrafish models with mutations in genes including ptk7 and col11a2 show spinal deformity. In mice, conditional deletion of Adgrg6 in cartilage produces progressive thoracic scoliosis with endplate herniations, demonstrating that cartilage and osteochondroprogenitor cells contribute to scoliosis phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 summarize prior animal model studies supported by citations (Hayes et al., 2014; Van Gennip et al., 2018; Rebello et al., 2023; Long et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021). These provide important context for the tissue-specific focus of the current study and support the hypothesis that cartilage defects contribute to spinal deformity.

results.result: Rare dominant mutations in COL11A1 can cause Marshall syndrome (MRSHS) or Stickler syndrome (STL2), which are characterized by various features including facial anomalies, hearing loss, short stature, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, eye anomalies, and scoliosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 describe established knowledge about COL11A1-related syndromes. This information is important for distinguishing the common AIS-associated variant from rare pathogenic mutations that cause syndromic forms of scoliosis.

results.result: Pax1 is a well-described marker of condensing sclerotomal cells during early spine development, activating a gene expression cascade starting at E12.5-13.5 in mouse development that leads to formation of the IVD and vertebrae.
results.evaluation: Claims C69 and C126 describe established knowledge about Pax1 function supported by citations (Chan et al., 2014; Aszódi et al., 1998; Smith et al., 2011; Wilm et al., 1998; Rodrigo et al., 2003; Sivakamasundari et al., 2017). This provides important developmental context for interpreting the Pax1 knockout experiments.

results.result: COL11A1 has been linked to ECM remodeling and invasiveness in cancers by enhancing MMP3 expression in response to TGFβ1. MMP3 (stromolysin) is an enzyme implicated in matrix degradation and remodeling in connective tissues, and is strongly expressed in human spinal cartilage and bone but minimally in muscle.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by citations (Wu et al., 2014; Mudgett et al., 1998) and RNAseq data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This provides rationale for investigating the COL11A1-MMP3 relationship in the context of AIS, though the relevance of cancer biology to AIS pathogenesis requires further validation.

results.result: The ATC (Acan enhancer-driven, doxycycline-inducible Cre) transgene shows recombination activity in differentiated chondrocytes and nucleus pulposus within 2 days of doxycycline treatment starting at E15.5, with strong Cre activity observed in P0 pups in the NP, CEP, AF of the IVD and in growth plate chondrocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by citation to Dy et al., 2012 and fluorescence imaging data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This validates the experimental approach for conditional deletion of Col11a1 in cartilage.

results.result: The AIS-associated P1335L variant occurs at the third position of a Gly-X-Y repeat in COL11A1 and is predicted to be deleterious by CADD (25.7) and GERP (5.75) analysis. It could be structurally important for triple helix stability, particularly if hydroxylated.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is an observation about the structural location of the variant. Claim C93 is supported by computational prediction scores. Claim C92 is speculative but reasonable given the location in a Gly-X-Y repeat. However, the authors acknowledge that low-resolution collagen structures limit detailed structural modeling, and the actual structural impact remains uncertain.

results.result: COL11A1 missense variants have been shown to evoke transcriptional changes in ECM genes in cancer cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021. This provides precedent for the observation that the P1335L variant affects gene expression, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: The expression of Col11a1 and other ECM genes is known to be estrogen-responsive in certain tissues such as ovarian follicular cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is supported by citation to Zalewski et al., 2012. This provides rationale for investigating estrogen receptor signaling in the context of Col11a1 regulation in chondrocytes.

results.result: Collagen type XI is a heterotrimer composed of chains encoded by COL11A1, COL11A2, and COL2A1, and is a minor but critical component of collagen type II fibrils in cartilage. It initiates fibrillogenesis, maintains fibril spacing and diameter, organizes the pericellular surface, and is broadly expressed in multiple tissues. In vitro, purified collagen XI stimulates chondrogenesis while inhibiting hypertrophy. Expression data suggest it participates in maintaining growth plate cells in a hypertrophic, pre-osteogenic state.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C120 describe established knowledge about collagen XI structure and function supported by citations and the authors' own expression data. This provides important biological context for interpreting the functional studies. The inference in C120 is reasonable based on the expression pattern data cited from Long et al., 2022 and personal communication.

results.result: Col11a1-deficient (cho/cho) mice show spinal deformities including incompletely formed vertebral bodies, spinal curvatures, decreased vertebral separation, and reduced mineralization. Common COL11A1 variants have been associated with lumbar disc herniation, disc degeneration, bone size, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis. These observations suggest that reduction in collagen type XI components disrupts spinal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by citations (Hafez et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2017; Mio et al., 2007; Styrkarsdottir et al., 2019). Claim C125 is an inference based on the cho/cho mouse model and zebrafish rescue experiments (Rebello et al., 2023), which is reasonable but would benefit from additional functional validation of the specific AIS-associated variant in vivo.

results.result: The downregulation of Col11a1 in Pax1-/- mice is consistent with prior studies. Col11a1 expression in developing tail is likely directly activated by SOX transcription factors, as super enhancers near Col11a1 were bound by SOX9 and SOX6 in rat chondrosarcoma cells. The SOX5/6/9 trio regulates many of the same genes as PAX1.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 are supported by citations (Sivakamasundari et al., 2017; Liu and Lefebvre, 2015). The inference in C128 is reasonable based on the ChIP-seq data, though direct evidence for SOX-mediated regulation of Col11a1 in the developmental context studied here is lacking. The relationship between PAX1 and SOX factors in regulating Col11a1 remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: The cartilage endplate is important for nutrient diffusion into the avascular IVD and harbors cells expressing type II collagen organized by collagen type XI. In humans, the endplate and vertebrae become separate structures at puberty. Lagging maturity of the ring apophysis combined with mechanical forces has been proposed as an initiating factor in AIS. Recently discovered vertebral skeletal stem cells (vSSCs) expressing Zic1, Pax1, and high levels of Col11a1 reside in the endplate, and AIS-associated variation in collagen α1(XI) could alter their differentiation trajectory.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C135 are supported by citations (Chan et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2011; Costa et al., 2021; Castelein et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023) and personal communication. However, claims C136 and C137 are speculative. While the localization data and vSSC findings are intriguing, direct evidence linking COL11A1 variation to altered vSSC differentiation or demonstrating that IVD-vertebral junction cells are causally involved in AIS pathogenesis is lacking. These represent important hypotheses for future investigation.

results.result: MMP3 (stromolysin) is a secreted enzyme expressed in connective tissues and endochondral ossification regions with degradative activity toward various ECM components (but not type I collagen). In chondrocytes, MMP3 translocates to the nucleus and activates transcription of CTGF/CCN2 by binding to TRENDIC. Col11a1 variation may have consequences for both MMP3 enzymatic activity and MMP3-mediated transcriptional programming.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C140 describe established knowledge about MMP3 function supported by citations (Ortega et al., 2004; Sellers and Murphy, 1981; Eguchi et al., 2008; Cui et al., 2017). Claim C141 is speculative but reasonable given the observed Col11a1-Mmp3 regulatory relationship. However, the manuscript does not directly test whether Col11a1 variation affects MMP3 enzymatic activity or nuclear translocation, only mRNA and protein levels.

results.result: COL11A1 missense variants altering glycine or proline in Gly-X-Y repeats are frequent in cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and have been linked to transcriptional changes and tumor invasiveness. The mechanisms by which cells sense single amino acid changes in collagen α1(XI) and induce transcriptional responses are unknown but may involve direct interaction with integrins in the pericellular space.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 are supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021. Claim C144 is speculative but represents a reasonable hypothesis. The manuscript does not investigate the mechanism by which the P1335L variant affects Mmp3 transcription, which remains an important question for future studies.

results.result: Type XI collagen is a key player in organizing the pericellular space, which is critical for transmitting mechanical forces from the ECM to the cell. Type XI collagen may effectively act as a receptor for environmental cues including mechanical forces and estrogen signaling in the adolescent spine.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2016. Claim C146 is speculative. While the data show that Col11a1 expression is sensitive to estrogen receptor signaling and that collagen XI organizes the pericellular space, the manuscript does not directly test whether collagen XI acts as a receptor for mechanical forces or integrate mechanical and hormonal signals. This represents an interesting hypothesis that requires further experimental validation.

results.result: The authors previously defined a female-specific AIS genetic risk locus in an enhancer near the PAX1 gene.
results.evaluation: Claim C3 refers to prior work by the authors (Sharma et al., 2015) and is supported by citation. This provides important context for the current study's investigation of PAX1 function.

results.result: PAX1 and collagen α1(XI) proteins both localize within the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region in postnatal spines, with less collagen α1(XI) detected in Pax1-/- spines compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 are supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A. The co-localization of PAX1 and collagen α1(XI) and the reduction of collagen α1(XI) in Pax1-/- mice provide important spatial and functional evidence linking these two proteins. However, the quantification of the reduction is qualitative rather than quantitative.

results.result: Wild-type Col11a1 expression in costal chondrocytes suppresses expression of Pax1 and Mmp3.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 are supported by qRT-PCR data from genetic targeting experiments. Claim C8 is supported by Figure 6B showing Pax1 upregulation after Col11a1 knockdown. Claim C9 is supported by Figures 4 and 5 showing Mmp3 upregulation after Col11a1 reduction. These findings establish bidirectional regulatory relationships between Pax1 and Col11a1, and between Col11a1 and Mmp3.

results.result: In cultured rat CEP cells, Esr2 and Mmp3 mRNA were downregulated and upregulated respectively after Col11a1 knockdown, similar to mouse chondrocytes. However, Esr2 knockdown did not significantly impact Col11a1 or Mmp3 expression in rat CEP cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C. The differential response to Esr2 knockdown between mouse chondrocytes and rat CEP cells suggests species or cell-type specificity in the estrogen-Col11a1-Mmp3 regulatory axis. This highlights a limitation in generalizing findings across species and cell types, and suggests that the regulatory mechanisms may be more complex than the proposed model indicates.

results.result: The authors identified a significant genetic association between the COL11A1 variant rs3753841 (p.Pro1335Leu) and AIS in a large multi-ethnic cohort (10,519 cases and 93,238 controls), with p=7.07E-11 and OR=1.118. The association remained significant in females when analyzed separately, while the MMP14 variant (rs1042704) did not show female-specific association.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledge and praise this genetic finding. Reviewer 1 states the study 'identifies an association with a variant in COL11A1 (Pro1335Leu)' and calls it 'valuable.' Reviewer 2 describes the work as 'nicely brings together an impressive number of human genetic data from multi-ethnic AIS cohorts' and notes the 'new AIS-associated coding variant in the COL11A1 gene.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'Col11a1P1335L is verified in multicenter cohorts with high confidence.' No concerns are raised about the genetic association data.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that PAX1 and collagen α1(XI) proteins colocalize in the intervertebral disc-vertebral junction region in postnatal mouse spines, with dramatically diminished collagen α1(XI) staining observed in Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms this finding, stating 'Using a Pax1 knockout mouse they go on to find that PAX1 and Collagen XI protein are expressed in the intervertebral discs (IVDs) and robustly in the growth plate, showing that COL11A1 expression is reduced in Pax1 mutant growth plate.' The immunofluorescence data supporting colocalization and reduction in Pax1-/- mice is accepted without critique.

results.result: The authors show that expression of Col11a1, Adgrg6, and Sox6 was significantly reduced in both female and male Pax1-/- mice compared to wild-type mice, suggesting that loss of Pax1 leads to reduced expression of these AIS-associated genes in affected tissue.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges this result: 'Moreover, other AIS-associated genes, Gpr126 and Sox6, were also reduced in Pax1 mutant mice, suggesting a common pathway is involved in AIS.' The qRT-PCR data showing reduced expression of these genes in Pax1-/- mice is accepted without challenge.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that wild-type Col11a1 expression in costal chondrocytes suppresses expression of Mmp3, as shown by increased Mmp3 mRNA and protein levels (2- to 5-fold) when Col11a1 is knocked down or deleted. This negative regulation was observed both in vitro and in vivo.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 confirms this finding: 'Using SV40 immortalized costal cartilage cells, derived from floxed Col11a1 mice primary rib cage cartilage, they go to show that removal of Col11a1 leads to reduction of Mmp3 expression' (note: the reviewer appears to have misstated 'reduction' when they meant 'increase,' but the overall acceptance of the Col11a1-Mmp3 relationship is clear). Reviewer 3 also acknowledges 'a Pax1-Col11a1-Mmp3 signaling axis.' The data is accepted without methodological critique.

results.result: The authors show that while overexpressing wild-type COL11A1 suppresses Mmp3 expression in mouse chondrocytes, the AIS-associated COL11A1P1335L mutant fails to downregulate Mmp3 expression, suggesting that regulation of Mmp3 is perturbed by this variant.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms: 'In this context, the expression of wild-type Col11a1 restored regular levels of Mmp3 expression, while expression of the AIS-associated Col11a1P1335L allele failed to restore normal Mmp3 expression. This supports a model that the AIS-associated Col11a1P1335L allele leads to the dysregulation of ECM in vivo.' Reviewer 3 states 'the authors have identified a new COL11A1 mutation and verified its effect on the Pax1-Col11a1-Mmp3 axis.' The functional validation is accepted.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that knockdown of the estrogen receptor gene Esr2 or tamoxifen treatment significantly alters Col11a1 and Mmp3 expression in mouse chondrocytes, with Esr2 knockdown leading to upregulation of Col11a1 and Pax1 and downregulation of Mmp3. The authors conclude that estrogen signaling suppresses Col11a1 expression and that ESR2 signaling disrupts the suppression of Mmp3 by Col11a1.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms: 'Using this culture system, they go on to test the role of the estrogen receptor ESR2, showing that loss of this receptor leads to reduced Mmp3 and Pax1 expression, and increased Col11a1 expression.' Reviewer 1 states the work 'suggests a connection between Pax1, Col11a1, Mmp3, and estrogen signaling, thus providing solid support for the proposed link between hormonal and matrix components.' Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'estrogen affects this signaling axis.' The estrogen-related findings are accepted.

results.result: The authors propose a new molecular model of AIS pathogenesis wherein genetic variation and estrogen signaling increase disease susceptibility by altering a PAX1-COL11a1-MMP3 signaling axis in spinal chondrocytes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the work 'provides solid support for the proposed link between hormonal and matrix components in the development of AIS.' Reviewer 2 describes the study as supporting 'a new molecular mechanism by which estrogen can interact and synergize with COL11A1/PAX1/MMP3 signaling to change ECM development and dynamics, thus providing a tangible model for mutations and dysregulation of this pathway can increase the susceptibility of scoliosis.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the article identified a potential pathogenesis of AIS.' The proposed model is accepted by all reviewers.

results.result: The authors analyzed RNAseq data from adolescent human spinal tissues and found that COL11A1 was upregulated in cartilage relative to bone and muscle, and that PAX1 and COL11A2 showed the strongest expression levels relative to other AIS-associated genes in cartilage.
results.evaluation: This expression analysis is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is presented as supporting data for the relevance of COL11A1 in cartilage. No reviewer raises concerns about this analysis, and it is consistent with the overall acceptance of the cartilage-focused findings.

results.result: The authors show through immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence that collagen α1(XI) is detectable in all compartments of young postnatal mouse IVD, with particularly abundant staining in the chondro-osseous junction region of IVD and vertebral growth plate, especially in pre-hypertrophic/hypertrophic chondrocytic cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges this localization data as part of the overall findings about PAX1 and Collagen XI protein expression in IVDs and growth plates. The immunohistochemistry data is accepted without critique and supports the relevance of the IVD-vertebral junction region in AIS pathogenesis.

results.result: The authors tested the Col11a1-Mmp3 relationship in cultured rat cartilage endplate (CEP) cells and found that Col11a1 knockdown led to upregulation of Mmp3 mRNA (as in mouse chondrocytes), but Esr2 knockdown did not significantly impact Col11a1 or Mmp3 expression in these cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 mentions 'They support this by showing similar gene expression changes and estrogen receptor function in Rat cartilage endplate cell culture,' but the actual data shows that Esr2 knockdown did NOT have the same effect in rat CEP cells as in mouse chondrocytes. This discrepancy is not explicitly addressed by reviewers, creating uncertainty about the generalizability of the estrogen signaling findings across cell types.

results.result: The authors report that their AIS cohort and individuals carrying the rs3753841 risk allele were negative for co-morbidities or obvious features of Marshall or Stickler syndromes, leading them to conclude that variation in COL11A1 is independently associated with AIS.
results.evaluation: This clinical observation is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is an important control to distinguish AIS-associated variants from syndromic mutations. No reviewer raises concerns about this claim, and it supports the independence of the COL11A1 association with AIS.

results.result: The authors generated Pax1-/- mice that were viable and developed spine deformity and kinks in the tail, with highly disorganized IVD lacking discernable NP, AF, and CEP structures.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges the use of 'a Pax1 knockout mouse' in the study. The phenotypic observations are consistent with prior reports and are accepted without critique as part of the validation of Pax1's role in spinal development.

results.result: Gene-set enrichment analysis of RNAseq from E12.5 Pax1-/- versus wild-type tail tissue was most significant for the gene ontology term 'extracellular matrix.'
results.evaluation: This gene ontology analysis is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but supports the ECM-focused interpretation of Pax1 function. No concerns are raised about this analysis.

results.result: The authors validated that Mmp3 mRNA and protein levels were significantly increased after Col11a1 knockdown in wild-type chondrocytes, detected Esr2 (but not Esr1) in mouse chondrocytes, and observed that Col11a1 knockdown upregulated Pax1 expression, suggesting a negative feedback loop between Pax1 and Col11a1.
results.evaluation: These findings are part of the overall accepted Col11a1-Mmp3-Pax1-Esr2 signaling axis. Reviewer 2 acknowledges the estrogen receptor work and the overall pathway. The negative feedback loop between Pax1 and Col11a1 is not explicitly discussed but is consistent with the accepted model.

results.result: The authors confirmed strong MMP3 mRNA expression in human spinal cartilage and bone, but minimal expression in spinal muscle.
results.evaluation: This expression analysis is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but provides supporting evidence for the relevance of MMP3 in cartilage and bone. No concerns are raised.

results.result: The authors observed that the proteolytic processing of precursor MMP3 into active forms did not appear to be affected by Col11a1 expression.
results.evaluation: This observation about MMP3 processing is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is a mechanistic detail that clarifies that Col11a1 affects MMP3 expression levels rather than processing. No concerns are raised.

results.result: The authors used an inducible ATC-Cre system to achieve Cre-mediated recombination in differentiated chondrocytes and NP, demonstrating strong Cre activity in P0 pups in the NP, CEP, and AF of the IVD and in chondrocytes of the growth plates.
results.evaluation: This methodological detail about the Cre system is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is part of the accepted in vivo validation of the Col11a1-Mmp3 relationship. Reviewer 2 notes the work 'functionally tests these findings in cell culture and animal models.' No concerns are raised about the Cre system.

results.result: The authors note that the AIS-associated variant P1335L occurs at the third position of a Gly-X-Y repeat in COL11A1 and speculate it could be structurally important in promoting stability of the collagen triple helix. They also report that the variant is predicted to be deleterious by CADD (25.7) and GERP (5.75) analysis.
results.evaluation: These structural and computational predictions are not explicitly discussed by reviewers but provide supporting evidence for the pathogenicity of the P1335L variant. Reviewer 1 describes the variant as 'potentially pathogenic,' consistent with these predictions. No concerns are raised.

results.result: The manuscript includes extensive background and contextual claims about AIS epidemiology, genetics, prior GWAS findings, animal models, collagen biology, MMP3 function, and speculative interpretations about mechanisms and cell populations relevant to AIS pathogenesis.
results.evaluation: These claims represent background knowledge, literature citations, and contextual framing that are not directly evaluated by reviewers but are accepted as part of the manuscript's scientific context. Reviewer 3 notes 'the significance of this work is high, especially given the still large knowledge gap of the mechanistic underpinnings for AIS,' acknowledging the importance of the background context. No specific concerns are raised about these contextual claims.

results.result: The authors reference their prior work defining a female-specific AIS genetic risk locus in an enhancer near the PAX1 gene.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges this: 'This revised study follows up on previous work showing a female-specific enhancer region of PAX1 is associated with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS).' This prior finding is accepted as the foundation for the current study.

comparisons.comparison: Both OpenEval and peer reviewers strongly support the genetic association findings (C4, C52-C55). All reviewers praise the multi-ethnic cohort data and statistical rigor. OpenEval additionally evaluates C58-C59 (independence from syndromic scoliosis), which peer reviewers accept implicitly in R11.

Perfect agreement on C10, C95-C97. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the functional validation showing that wild-type COL11A1 restores normal MMP3 expression while the P1335L variant fails to do so. Both acknowledge this as key evidence linking the variant to disease mechanism.

Complete agreement on C15. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the integrative model connecting genetic association, expression studies, regulatory relationships, and estrogen signaling. All reviewers view this as a valuable contribution to understanding AIS pathogenesis.

Strong agreement on C11-C14, C99-C107, C111 regarding estrogen receptor signaling. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers accept the evidence that ESR2 modulates the Col11a1-Mmp3 pathway. OpenEval notes species/cell-type specificity limitations (C108-C110), which peer reviewer R10 acknowledges with uncertainty.

Both support C5-C7 showing PAX1 and collagen XI colocalization and reduction in Pax1-/- mice. Peer reviewer R2 explicitly confirms these immunofluorescence findings. OpenEval notes the quantification is qualitative rather than quantitative.

Both support C76-C79 showing reduced expression of AIS-associated genes (Gpr126, Sox6) in Pax1 mutant mice. Peer reviewer R2 explicitly acknowledges this qRT-PCR data. OpenEval provides broader evaluation including C70-C75 (knockout phenotype, immunofluorescence, RNAseq, GO analysis), which peer reviewers address separately in R12 and R13.

Both support the Col11a1-Mmp3 regulatory relationship (C84-C87, C90). Peer reviewer R2 confirms the finding though misstates 'reduction' instead of 'increase' in MMP3. OpenEval also evaluates C8-C9 (bidirectional regulation), which peer reviewers address in R14.

Both support C60-C62 showing COL11A1 expression in cartilage by RNAseq. Peer reviewers do not explicitly discuss this but accept it as supporting data. OpenEval also evaluates C63-C68 (immunohistochemistry localization), which peer reviewers address in R9.
